story_text.value:
Dualayer Hierarchy Standard (DHS:

Repo: https://github.com/Zainium-Dynamics/dualayer-hierarchy-stand... Full Specification (23-page PDF): https://zainiumdynamics.tech/dhs

DHS 1.1 defines a layered filesystem hierarchy for immutable Linux systems where musl and glibc coexist side by side without conflict. Either C library can be primary; the distribution chooses.

Root layout (no /usr, /bin, /sbin, /lib, /lib64, /etc, /var, or /boot at /, not even as symlinks):

  /
  |-- overlayer/   (the entire OS: all layers)
  |-- home/        (user home directories)
  |-- root/        (root home)
  |-- dev/         (devtmpfs)
  |-- proc/        (procfs)
  |-- sys/         (sysfs)
  |-- run/         (tmpfs; removable media at /run/media/user/label)
  `-- tmp/         (temporary files)
Layer structure under /overlayer (composed at boot via OverlayFS with syshub as lower and userland/union as upper):

  /overlayer/
  |-- syshub/           (read-only base OS; boots without userland)
  |-- userland/         (installed packages: union/, work/, registry/)
  |-- ignition/         (kernels, initramfs, bootloader; read-only)
  |-- agents/           (optional AI coding agent instructions/policies)
  `-- .syshub-pending/  (staged atomic base upgrade, applied at next boot)
Dual-libc isolation: musl and glibc each live in their own GNU target-triplet directory (arch-vendor-linux-musl and arch-vendor-linux-gnu) with separate loaders, headers, C++ runtimes, loader configs, and toolchains. Shared directories (/overlayer/syshub/bin, lib, include) belong strictly to the primary libc and search paths never cross, while both read shared system config (passwd, hosts, resolv.conf, zoneinfo) from /overlayer/syshub/etc.

FHS compatibility: Foreign packages are adapted at install time (PT_INTERP, RPATH, pkg-config, shebangs). Runtime FHS path lookups use a preload resolver and loader redirection (the known LD_PRELOAD limitation for static/setuid binaries is documented in Chapter 7).

Reference implementation — Zainium OS (https://github.com/Zainium-Dynamics): - Layers: syshub (base), zexlib (userland), zaisys (ignition) - Libc design: Design A (musl primary in base, glibc as a userland package) - Boot & atomic upgrades: quantra-ramfs - Package manager & receipts: zex - Path/loader resolver & toolchain switcher: libsys_resolver.so, sys-resolver - Protected base/ignition paths: elevate, elevate-pam

Looking for honest technical critique on where this layout holds up, where it breaks down, and what edge cases are missing.

title.value: Show HN: Dualayer Hierarchy Standard (DHS) – Zero-FHS Layout for Musl and Glibc

story_text.value:
Economic calendar? Subscription. Company earnings schedule and expected move? Subscription. Options positioning data? Subscription. SEC filings? Subscription.

And the list goes on. That's just too many subscriptions and browser tabs for me and my day to day market research hobby.

I'm building a single workspace to unify it all. Markets, stocks, options, fillings, insider trades including congress, etf breakdown, macro indicators by country etc.

No ads, no 4 different tiers of subscriptions, no snake oil predictions and 'trust my model' nonsense. You get the data. You make the call.

Check it out here: https://app.trenchesterminal.com/ It's still work in progress, some pages are rougher than others. Some data might be delayed and or incomplete.

Happy to hear any feedback!

story_text.value:
I was fed up with IPython and the default Python, editing more than one line is painful. But Jupyter and marimo both need a server and a browser tab just to try an idea. I wanted a notebook that opens like a vim does

So I built gpython. It is a notebook in the terminal, built on Textual. Cells are reactive like marimo and has vim keys. You can open both ipynb and .py files like marimo supports. It also has image support for supported terminals and is the fastest among marimo and jupyter based on our limited benchmark test.

Try it without installing: uvx --from gpynb gpython

It is early (0.2.3). I would love feedback on it's usability. And I am curious: would you use this in place of IPython or Jupyter for quick work? If not, what is missing?

title.value: Show HN: Gpython – A Terminal based notebook for Python

Hey guys,

Long time lurker, first time poster.

I had some...well lets just say, "speed bumps" in my life that prevented me from getting this out sooner.

I've had this idea for years but it finally all came together recently. I was big into R/C racing before drones and FPV became cool. I kept seeing all the proprietary cameras and headsets and thought why cant we use the current VR headsets as FPV controllers or even our phones.

So I built some stuff. At the moment I am putting these together by hand and honestly I'm still working out some bugs but I just wanted to put it out there and see what happens.

Thanks! -P

PS - if anyone knows James Cameron feel free to share this.

story_text.value:
fmgrep is a (Claude-powered) open source reimplementation of a FAANG code search engine I was involved in a few years back. It's aimed at very large (e.g. AOSP) source trees.

Back then we wanted to get our hands on the Github search engine (https://github.com/danlark1/sparse_ngrams) but it was not available, so we went a different way.

Instead of n-grams,`fmgrep` builds an FM index of the tree with O(pattern) `count` and O(occurrences) `locate`, which is quite cool and leads to blazing fast performance as seen in the benchmarks.

title.value: Show HN: Fmgrep – indexed grep over a persistent FM index
